scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that expertise is indispensable for technical judgment while arguing that much valuable judgment is non-expert and that the right judge depends on the question; coherent and persuasive.

sentences.text: When a critic pans a film or a layperson questions a scientific theory, we often ask: what gives them the right, if they are not experts?
The statement answers firmly, holding that critical judgment of work in any field has little value unless it comes from an expert in that field.

Expertise certainly improves certain kinds of judgment, but the statement goes too far, because much valuable criticism comes from non-experts, and some fields exist precisely to be judged by ordinary people.
It is true that for many judgments, expertise is indispensable.
Only someone trained in a field fully understands its problems, methods, and standards, and can tell a genuine advance from a plausible-looking error.
A non-physicist cannot meaningfully judge whether a new theory is sound, and a patient cannot assess a surgeon's technique the way another surgeon can.
For technical correctness — is this proof valid, this diagnosis right, this engineering safe — the informed judgment of experts is worth far more than the opinion of the crowd.
So the statement is right that, on questions of technical merit, expert judgment carries a weight amateur judgment cannot.

sections.role: Body — But much valuable judgment is not expert

sentences.text: However, to say that non-expert judgment has little value ignores how much of it is both valid and necessary.
A great deal of work is made for ordinary people, and on whether it succeeds for them, ordinary people are the real experts.

A film, a novel, a product, or a building is judged in part by how it affects its audience or users, and their response — does it move me, does it work for me — is not an amateur error but the very point.
The fresh eye of an outsider can also catch what insiders, deep in their assumptions, have stopped seeing, which is why fields often benefit from external criticism.
Even on technical matters, history shows experts collectively mistaken, their consensus corrected by an outsider or by results no credential could override.
Valuable judgment, in short, is not the monopoly of experts.
The diner, not only the chef, can tell whether the meal is any good.

sections.role: Body — Match the judge to the question

sentences.text: Moreover, the truth is that different judgments call for different judges.
On questions of technical correctness, defer to experts; on questions of value, usefulness, or human effect, the audience's judgment may matter more.
The statement errs by treating all critical judgment as the kind only experts can offer, when much of what is worth judging is precisely how work serves the non-experts it is meant for.
A wise field listens to experts on its methods and to everyone on its purposes, rather than dismissing all outside voices as worthless.
Expertise should inform judgment, not monopolize it.
In conclusion, expert judgment is invaluable on technical questions but far from the only judgment that has value.
Because much work exists to serve non-experts and outsiders sometimes see what insiders miss, critical judgment from beyond the field is often essential, not worthless.
The right question is not whether a critic is an expert, but whether their judgment fits the kind of question being asked.
